facts.capital: Phoenix (the most populous state capital in the U.S.)
facts.statehood_note: Arizona was the 48th state and the last of the 48 contiguous (connected) states to join the Union.
facts.nickname: The Grand Canyon State (also called the Copper State, because by 1907 Arizona produced more copper than any other state)
borders: Colorado (touches only at the Four Corners)
Mexico (the states of Sonora and Baja California)
facts.name_origin: The name most likely comes from the O'odham words alĭ ṣonak, meaning "small spring," which Spanish settlers heard as "Arissona." A less-supported idea links it to a Basque phrase meaning "the good oak."

government.chambers: Arizona Senate (30 members) and Arizona House of Representatives (60 members). Each of the 30 legislative districts elects one senator and two representatives. Members may serve up to four terms in a row (eight years) in each house.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; no more than two terms in a row). The governor commands the state's military forces (except when they are called into federal service), can veto bills, and can grant pardons. In 2022 voters approved Proposition 131, which created the office of Lieutenant Governor, elected on a joint ticket with the governor. Voters choose the first lieutenant governor in the November 2026 election, and the office begins on January 4, 2027; the lieutenant governor then replaces the Secretary of State as first in line to succeed the governor. Until then, Arizona has no lieutenant governor and the Secretary of State is first in line.
government.courts: Arizona Supreme Court (7 justices: a chief justice, a vice chief justice, and five associate justices, serving six-year terms) is the highest court. Below it is the Court of Appeals in two divisions (Division One in Phoenix with 16 judges and Division Two in Tucson with 6 judges), then superior courts, justice courts, and city courts.
government.local: 15 counties (Maricopa County is the largest). Each county elects a sheriff, county attorney, recorder, treasurer, assessor, school superintendent, and at least three supervisors. Arizona's 22 federally recognized tribes are sovereign nations with their own governments.
government.constitution: Written at a constitutional convention of 52 delegates in 1910. President William H. Taft vetoed statehood because the constitution let voters recall (remove) judges; the delegates took that part out, and Arizona became a state on February 14, 1912. Soon after, the legislature proposed putting judicial recall back, and voters approved it in the 1912 general election. The constitution lets citizens propose laws (initiative), vote on laws (referendum), and recall elected officers.
government.kid_line: "Every person may freely speak, write, and publish on all subjects, being responsible for the abuse of that right." (Arizona Constitution, Article II, Section 6)

long_ago.about: Indigenous hunter-gatherers arrived in what is now Arizona more than 12,000 years ago.

For hundreds of years the Hohokam lived in villages near the Salt and Gila rivers, traded over long distances, and built large irrigation systems without metal tools. The word "Hohokam" comes from an Akimel O'odham term meaning "those who have gone," and Arizona's four southern tribes and some Pueblo tribes claim Hohokam ancestry.
The Hopi settled on mesas in northern Arizona by the 1100s. The Hopi village of Oraibi dates to at least 1150 CE.
The Diné arrived in the Southwest roughly 800 to 1,000 years ago. After the Spanish arrived in the mid-1500s, they took up raising livestock.
These ancient cultures also flourished in Arizona; their pueblos, cliffside homes, and rock paintings can still be seen today.

today.about: Based in Window Rock, Arizona; the Diné returned to part of their homeland under the 1868 treaty.

An O'odham nation based in Sells, Arizona.

first_peoples.today_note: The Arizona Department of Education lists 22 federally recognized tribes in Arizona, including the Ak-Chin Indian Community, Cocopah Indian Tribe, Colorado River Indian Tribes, Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation, Fort Mojave Indian Tribe, Fort Yuma-Quechan Indian Tribe, Hualapai Tribe, Kaibab Band of Paiute Indians, Pueblo of Zuni, San Carlos Apache Tribe, San Juan Southern Paiute, Tonto Apache Tribe, Yavapai-Apache Nation, and Yavapai-Prescott Indian Tribe, along with the eight above. Each is a sovereign nation with its own government.
sites: Casa Grande Ruins National Monument, Coolidge (a four-story Hohokam "great house" built about 1100 to 1300 from caliche; protected since 1892)
Oraibi, a Hopi village on the Hopi mesas, lived in since at least 1150 (visit only as the Hopi Tribe allows)

history.event: Indigenous hunter-gatherers live in what is now Arizona.
During the Hohokam Classic Period, people build the Casa Grande ("great house") near the Gila River and farm the desert with large irrigation systems.
The Hopi village of Oraibi is founded on the mesas of northern Arizona.
Fray Marcos de Niza, a Spanish priest searching for the legendary "Seven Golden Cities of Cibola," leads the first European expedition into the area.
Francisco Vázquez de Coronado's Spanish expedition crosses the region looking for gold; it is the first European group to see the Grand Canyon.

Jesuit priest Eusebio Francisco Kino starts a chain of missions in the Pimería Alta to convert Indigenous people of the Pimería Alta to Christianity; Franciscans take over after the Jesuits are expelled in 1767.
Spain builds military forts called presidios at Tubac (1752) and Tucson (1775).
Mexico wins independence from Spain, and the land that is now Arizona becomes part of Mexico.
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ends the U.S.-Mexican War and gives part of Arizona to the United States.
In the Gadsden Purchase, the United States buys the rest of southern Arizona from Mexico.
Civil War: the Confederacy declares its own "Territory of Arizona" on January 18, and the Battle of Picacho Pass becomes the westernmost Civil War fight on record.
On February 24, the United States creates the Arizona Territory; Prescott becomes the first territorial capital in 1864.

Kit Carson leads a scorched-earth campaign against the Diné (Navajo), and the U.S. Army forces them from their homeland on the Long Walk; many Diné die. The 1868 treaty lets the Diné return to their homeland and sets up a reservation.
A silver boom grows Tombstone; copper mining towns such as Bisbee and Jerome follow by the late 1880s.

trailblazers.name: Ira Hayes
trailblazers.text: Born in Sacaton on the Gila River Indian Reservation, Ira Hayes joined the Marine Corps Reserve in Phoenix in 1942. He landed on Iwo Jima on February 19, 1945, and was one of the Marines in the famous flag raising there. He is buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

trailblazers.name: Annie Dodge Wauneka
trailblazers.text: In 1951 Annie Dodge Wauneka became the second woman elected to the Navajo Tribal Council, where she led its Health and Welfare Committee for three terms. She worked to wipe out tuberculosis on the Navajo Nation. In 1963 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Lyndon B. Johnson.

trailblazers.name: Ayra Hackett
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, publisher and community leader
trailblazers.text: Ayra Hackett, a businesswoman, midwife, and community leader, founded the Arizona Gleam newspaper in Phoenix in November 1929. It served Phoenix's Black community, and she was the only Black newspaper owner in Arizona at the time. Even under segregation and Jim Crow laws, she grew the paper to cover national and world news.

trailblazers.name: Dr. Winston C. Hackett
trailblazers.text: Winston Hackett came to Phoenix in 1916 and became Arizona's first African American doctor. In 1922 he opened Booker T. Washington Memorial Hospital, the first hospital in Phoenix to serve the Black community, together with his wife, Ayra Hackett.

trailblazers.name: Lorna Lockwood
trailblazers.text: Born in Douglas, Arizona, Lorna Lockwood was elected to the Arizona House of Representatives in 1939 and later served as a Maricopa County Superior Court judge. Elected to the Arizona Supreme Court in 1960, she became the first woman Chief Justice of a state supreme court in U.S. history.

trailblazers.name: Raúl Héctor Castro
trailblazers.group: Mexican American man, governor and ambassador
trailblazers.text: Born in Cananea, Sonora, Mexico, he grew up in Pirtleville near Douglas, Arizona, and became a U.S. citizen in 1939. He worked as a lawyer, Pima County attorney, judge, and U.S. ambassador to El Salvador and Bolivia, and in 1974 he became the first Mexican American elected governor of Arizona. He later served as U.S. ambassador to Argentina.

landforms: Mogollon Rim (a cliff edge almost 2,000 feet high at the plateau's southwestern edge)
Basin and Range region (desert mountains and valleys in the south)
Grand Canyon (about 277 miles long and more than 1 mile deep)
waters: Colorado River (carved the Grand Canyon; its lowest point in Arizona, 72 feet, is at the Mexico border)
geography.regions: Arizona has the high Colorado Plateau in the north, separated by the Mogollon Rim from the Basin and Range deserts of the south.

ecosystems.name: Sonoran Desert
ecosystems.about: Southern Arizona's desert is filled with plants built to save water, such as cactus. Saguaro National Park near Tucson has the world's largest collection of saguaro cacti, and the saguaro blossom is the state flower.

ecosystems.name: Ponderosa pine forests
ecosystems.about: About 27% of Arizona is forest, and the state has the world's largest stand of ponderosa pine trees.

ecosystems.name: Grand Canyon and the Colorado River
ecosystems.about: Over a very long time the Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon, which is more than a mile deep; President Theodore Roosevelt made it a national monument in 1908.

science.weather: Low deserts have hot summers and mild winters. Arizona gets two rainy seasons: winter storms from the Pacific and the summer North American monsoon, whose storms can cause deadly flash floods. Wildfires are a serious hazard, such as the 2002 Rodeo-Chediski Fire.
science.resources: Arizona's early economy was known for the "five C's": copper, cotton, cattle, citrus, and climate. Copper is still a giant resource (about two-thirds of the nation's copper), and farms grow durum wheat, lettuce, and cantaloupe; today health care, transportation, and government are the biggest job areas.
science.highlight: Meteor Crater formed about 50,000 years ago when a space rock struck northern Arizona; the crater is nearly a mile wide and 570 feet deep.

g3_ss.title: Arizona's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Phoenix, Tucson, Arizona's 15 counties, and tribal nations on a map; learn what the governor, the 90-member legislature, and the 7-justice Supreme Court do; read Article II, Section 6 about free speech.

g3_ss.title: Arizona's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Hohokam farmers of Casa Grande, the Hopi of Oraibi, and the Diné, and learn that Arizona has 22 sovereign tribal nations today.

g3_ss.title: Arizona Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Make trading cards for Ira Hayes, Annie Dodge Wauneka, Ayra and Winston Hackett, Lorna Lockwood, and Raúl Castro, and tell how each one helped their community.

g45_ss.title: Arizona's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Compare Hohokam irrigation farming, Hopi mesa villages, and Diné herding, and trace today's 22 nations back to their homelands.

g45_ss.title: Spanish and Mexican Arizona
g45_ss.plan: Follow Marcos de Niza, Coronado, Kino's missions, and the Tubac and Tucson presidios, looking honestly at how missions changed O'odham lives; then see Arizona become part of Mexico in 1821.

g45_ss.title: Arizona 1848 to 1877
g45_ss.plan: Map the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo and the Gadsden Purchase, study Picacho Pass and the 1863 territory, and learn about the Long Walk and the 1868 Navajo treaty.

g3_sci.title: The Sonoran Desert
g3_sci.plan: Study how saguaros, palo verde trees, and cactus wrens survive heat and little rain.

g3_sci.title: Monsoon Season
g3_sci.plan: Track summer monsoon storms, learn why flash floods are dangerous, and make a family safety plan.

g3_sci.title: The Grand Canyon
g3_sci.plan: Model how a river carves rock over a very long time, using sand and water trays.

g45_sci.title: Meteor Crater
g45_sci.plan: Drop objects into flour to model impact craters, then compare with Meteor Crater's size (nearly a mile wide, 570 feet deep).

g45_sci.title: Copper and the Five C's
g45_sci.plan: Explore copper as a natural resource, how mining changed towns like Bisbee and Jerome, and how resources shape an economy.

g45_sci.title: Forests, Fire, and Water
g45_sci.plan: Compare ponderosa pine forests and deserts, and investigate wildfire and how Hohokam irrigation used river water in a dry land.
